content.title: About
content.content: Carrots, frozen, cooked with oil are a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh carrots that are blanched, flash‑frozen and then sautéed in vegetable oil. They retain a bright orange colour, a sweet taste and a crisp texture, making them convenient for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots have been cultivated for over 5,000 years and are among the world’s most popular vegetables.
Freezing preserves up to 90 % of vitamin A and beta‑carotene, which give carrots their vivid colour and eye‑health benefits.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin E and carotenoids.
Frozen vegetables are widely used in restaurants and cafeterias to speed up cooking.
In many countries carrots are frozen as cubes or slices, which makes them easy to add to soups and stews.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted in the body to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carrots provide vitamin C, vitamin E and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fibre in carrots promotes regular bowel movements and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: May reduce cardiovascular risk
items.content: Potassium and antioxidants help regulate blood pressure and protect blood vessels.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Carrots contain modest amounts of calcium and magnesium, important for bone maintenance.

items.title: Carrot allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to carrots, ranging from itching to swelling.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: The sweet taste comes from natural sugars; individuals with diabetes should consider the carbohydrate content.

items.title: Added oil
items.content: Since the product is cooked with oil, those monitoring fat intake should account for the extra calories.

items.title: Vitamin loss over time
items.content: Prolonged storage in the freezer can lead to a slight decrease in vitamin C levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen carrots cooked with oil can be tossed into soups, stews, pasta, rice dishes, or used as a quick side for meat and fish. Heat them in a pan, microwave, or add directly to hot dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, use within 3–4 months for best quality. Do not thaw and refreeze to avoid texture and flavor degradation.

content.title: About
content.content: Champagne Punch is a refreshing cocktail made with sparkling champagne, fruit juices, and a light syrup. It blends the effervescence of champagne with bright citrus and berry flavors, sometimes enhanced with spices, creating a festive drink ideal for celebrations and parties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Punch originated in England in the 18th century as a way to stretch expensive spirits.
The classic recipe combines champagne, lemon and orange juice, and a touch of sugar.
In the United States, champagne punch gained popularity during Prohibition in the 1920s as a non‑alcoholic alternative.
Many variations exist, adding berries, mint, ginger ale, or even rose‑flavored champagne.
Punch is often served in large pitchers, allowing guests to pour their own glasses.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Citrus juices are rich in vitamin C and flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: The majority of the drink is water from champagne and juices, contributing to fluid balance.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing
items.content: Moderate champagne consumption can trigger endorphin release, improving mood.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Champagne contains alcohol; excessive intake can lead to intoxication and related hazards.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Syrup and fruit juices raise sugar levels, which may be problematic for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some recipes include berries or spices that can cause allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve Champagne Punch chilled in champagne flutes or coupe glasses. Add lemon and orange slices, fresh berries, and a sprig of mint for garnish. Ice can be used if desired, but it may dilute the effervescence.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared punch in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours to preserve fruit freshness and champagne fizz. Seal the container tightly to prevent absorption of other odors.

cheese-flavored-corn-snacks-reduced-fat.title: Cheese flavored corn snacks, reduced fat

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese flavored corn snacks with reduced fat are crunchy bites made from whole‑grain corn flour, seasoned with natural cheese flavor and containing minimal fat. They are ideal for people watching their calorie intake while still craving a rich, savory taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The snacks are produced by extrusion, which preserves most of corn’s natural nutrients.
Cheese flavor is achieved using real dairy proteins and natural flavorings, without artificial colorants.
Fat reduction is accomplished by replacing part of the vegetable oil with air‑puffing technology.
The corn used is often non‑GMO and sourced from sustainable farms.
These snacks are commonly part of the “light” and “healthy snack” lines of major manufacturers.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes the product more suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn flour provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and regularity.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: The snack causes a gradual rise in blood sugar, which is convenient for those monitoring glycemia.

items.title: Dairy protein allergy
items.content: The cheese component may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; people on low‑sodium diets should watch portion size.

items.title: Not gluten‑free
items.content: Although corn‑based, processing may involve gluten‑containing additives.

items.title: Caloric density in large portions
items.content: Despite reduced fat, the snack is still calorie‑dense; overeating can lead to excess energy intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the snacks straight from the bag, toss them into salads, use as a crunchy topping for soups, or pair with yogurt for a savory dip. For extra flavor, lightly warm them in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original packaging or an airtight container. For extended shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain crunch and prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Processed cheese is a product made by melting natural cheese together with emulsifiers, salt, flavorings and sometimes added milk fats. It has a smooth, uniform texture, slices easily and melts quickly, making it popular in sandwiches, sauces and hot dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first industrial processed cheese was developed in Switzerland at the end of the 19th century.
Emulsifiers such as sodium phosphate salts keep the cheese homogeneous even at high temperatures.
Processed cheese is widely used in fast‑food because of its rapid meltability and long shelf life.
The product has different names worldwide: in the US – processed cheese, in Russia – плавленый сыр, in Japan – チーズスナック.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Provides a notable amount of calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Delivers complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The smooth texture makes it gentle on the digestive system, especially for children and the elderly.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Offers quick energy through a combination of fats and carbohydrates.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Elevated salt levels can contribute to high blood pressure and fluid retention.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Contains saturated fatty acids, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or lactose may experience reactions.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Often includes food additives that may be undesirable for those with sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Processed cheese is convenient sliced for sandwiches, grated into hot sauces, added to casseroles, omelets and pizza. It is also sold as meltable sticks and snack portions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2 °C–6 °C. Shelf life is indicated on the label; after opening, use within 2–3 weeks. Discard if any mold, off‑odor, or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: A macchiato is an espresso “stained” with a small amount of foamed milk. The sweetened version contains added sugar or syrup, giving the drink a smoother, more aromatic profile. The coffee base is usually a medium‑roasted Arabica, offering fruity and nutty notes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “macchiato” comes from Italian meaning “spotted” or “stained”.
The first macchiato recipe appeared in Italy in the early 1920s.
Sweetened macchiatos are often served with flavored syrups such as vanilla, caramel, or hazelnut.
In Japan a popular “sweet macchiato” includes a drizzle of sweet soy paste (mochi).
Coffee macchiato is frequently used as a flavor base for desserts and sauces.

items.title: Energizing effect
items.content: Caffeine in espresso stimulates the central nervous system, enhancing alertness and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine can modestly boost metabolic rate and aid fat oxidation when consumed in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee provides small amounts of vitamins B2, B3, and B5, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Caffeine increases dopamine and serotonin levels, which may improve mood.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened drinks add extra calories and can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain stimulants and reduce the efficacy of sedatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweetened macchiato is served hot in small cups (≈150 ml). You can add a flavored syrup, sprinkle cinnamon or cocoa powder, or serve it over ice for a cold version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store freshly roasted ground coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dark place, using it within 2‑3 weeks. Milk should be used fresh, and a prepared drink should not be kept longer than 1‑2 hours at room temperature.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-potatoe.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with potatoes and/or onions, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs, boiled or baked potatoes and onions, prepared without added oil or other fats. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while potatoes and onions supply carbohydrates, fiber, vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are often called a “complete food” because they contain all essential amino acids.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed vegetables and are rich in vitamin C and potassium.
Onions contain sulfur compounds that give them their characteristic aroma and have antioxidant properties.
Cooking without fat preserves the natural taste of the ingredients and results in a low‑energy‑density meal.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: One serving provides about 6 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in vitamin D and B12
items.content: The yolk supplies vitamin D, while both yolk and white contain vitamin B12, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes and onions are good sources of potassium and magnesium, which help heart and muscle function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Potato skins and onions add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low added fat
items.content: Absence of oil reduces saturated fat and overall calorie content.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Solanine in potatoes
items.content: Green spots or sprouts can contain solanine, a toxin that should be avoided.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Boil or bake potatoes until tender, dice them. Sauté onions in a dry pan until golden (add a splash of water if needed). Beat the eggs, pour them over the vegetables, and stir continuously until the mixture sets. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat with a little water to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain restructured potato chips are a light, crunchy snack made from whole potatoes, whole grains (oats, corn, rice) and a small amount of plant protein. The restructuring technology binds the ingredients into a single matrix, preserving the classic potato flavor while adding the nutritional benefits of grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Restructured chips contain up to 30 % whole grains, increasing fiber compared with regular potato chips.
The technology reduces the amount of added oil without sacrificing crispness.
The multigrain blend often includes oats, which are rich in beta‑glucan – a soluble fiber beneficial for heart health.
Chips are made without artificial flavors or colorings; taste comes from natural potato aroma and light toasting of the grains.
In some countries these chips are classified as a “semi‑finished product,” simplifying import procedures.

items.title: Higher fiber content
items.content: Whole grains boost dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low trans‑fat levels
items.content: Restructuring allows the use of plant oils low in trans fats, which is heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Oats and corn provide slow‑release energy, helping maintain satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Grains supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Potato and oat polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Grain allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to oats, corn, or rice and should avoid the product.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Like most chips, it can contain a notable amount of salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite reduced oil, the snack remains energy‑dense and can contribute to weight gain if over‑consumed.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: If oats are included, the product may contain trace gluten, important for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the chips straight from the bag, toss them into salads for crunch, use as a garnish for soups, or serve with dips such as yogurt‑based sauces, guacamole, or hummus.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the chips in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, transfer to an airtight container to maintain crispness.

seafood-garden-salad-with-seafood-lettuc.title: Seafood Garden Salad with Seafood, Lettuce, Eggs, and Vegetables (no tomato, no carrots)

content.title: About
content.content: The Seafood Garden Salad combines fresh seafood (shrimp, squid, mussels), crisp lettuce, hard‑boiled eggs, and a variety of vegetables (cucumber, bell pepper, radish). The recipe excludes tomatoes and carrots and is served without dressing, letting the natural flavors shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seafood is a rich source of omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and brain health.
Eggs add protein and a bright yellow hue, making the dish visually appealing.
Leafy lettuce (romaine, iceberg, mixed greens) stays crunchy due to its low water content.
Omitting tomatoes reduces acidity, which can be easier on sensitive stomachs.
The salad is often featured in coastal restaurants as a light starter or a light main course.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Shrimp, mussels and squid provide EPA and DHA, which help reduce inflammation and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and seafood together deliver a complete amino‑acid profile for muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The salad supplies B12, B6 and niacin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains zinc, iron, selenium and iodine, nutrients important for immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The large volume of vegetables and lettuce keeps the dish light, suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or squid.

items.title: Raw eggs
items.content: If eggs are not fully cooked, there is a risk of salmonella contamination.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using pre‑cooked or canned seafood can increase the salt level of the salad.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain seafood may contain trace amounts of mercury; choose reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, straight after assembly. It can be enjoyed on its own or alongside whole‑grain bread. If desired, a light lemon‑olive‑oil drizzle may be added, though the classic version is served without dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Longer storage may cause the seafood to lose freshness and the lettuce to become soggy.
